book.summary: Dirk Laukens's Complete Chord Melody is a 5-module + 2-appendix course for solo and trio chord-melody jazz guitar. Module 1 Quickstart establishes the 4-step arranging workflow (tune choice → key → melody on top strings → chord voicings beneath). Module 2 Chord Vocabulary builds chord collections for the three harmonic families via the ii-V-I progression, including 2nd-string voicing variants and minor ii-V-i with m7b5 + 7alt. Module 3 walks the Autumn Leaves arrangement end-to-end. Module 4 expands to solo guitar techniques (diads, walking bass, passing chords, intros/endings/fills). Module 5 covers advanced reharmonization (back cycling, common-tone substitution) and performance preparation (3-stage metronome practice, rubato on substitutions). Appendix 1 is a chord dictionary; Appendix 2 is a fingerstyle technique etude collection.

chapter.title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
chapter.summary: Module 3 of Laukens' Complete Chord Melody course walks through the full process of harmonising a melody against a chord progression, using Fly Me to the Moon as the primary vehicle. It covers interval analysis of melody notes against chords, the chord-dictionary lookup method for selecting voicings, playability trade-offs, adding tension to dominant chords, and two complete worked arrangements (Fly Me to the Moon and Alone Together). Pages 137–180 introduce solo guitar arranging concepts: bass-line integration, shell voicings, open-string key selection, arpeggiation, octaves, and diads — all illustrated with Moon River and other standards.

sections.title: Making Arrangements Playable — Density, Voicing Cuts, and Alternatives
sections.summary: Counterbalances the chord-dictionary enthusiasm: placing chords on every melody note is a common beginner mistake. Less is more. When a voicing is mechanically difficult, three solutions exist: (1) cut low/unnecessary notes from the chord, (2) replace block chords with diads or octaves, (3) remove the chord entirely. Option 3 is often most effective for hand relaxation and musical flow.

sections.title: Introduction to Solo Guitar Arranging
sections.summary: Frames the conceptual shift from trio chord melody to solo guitar: the arranger must now imply bass, rhythm, and melody simultaneously. The key insight is that all three need only be *suggested*, not constantly present. Alternating bass lines, chord lines, and single-note lines creates the illusion of a full band. Pick vs. fingerstyle is addressed (fingerstyle strongly preferred for simultaneous voicing notes). Key selection favouring open strings (A, E, D) reduces fretting complexity and extends bass register.

7th string George Van Eps Lenny Breau

sections.title: Arpeggiation, Octaves, and Diads
sections.summary: Three texture-generation tools beyond block chords: (1) Arpeggiation — notes of a chord plucked sequentially, adds lyricism especially in ballads. (2) Octaves — Wes Montgomery's device of doubling the melody one octave below, played with a strum or individual plucking, muting the intervening string with the first finger. (3) Diads — Barney Kessel's harmonic-line technique, parallelising the melody in 3rds or 6ths. All three serve to create textural variety and reduce technical demands in fast passages.

sections.title: Walking Bass Techniques
sections.summary: Step-by-step construction of a walking bass line for solo guitar: place root on beat 1, add approach note on beat 4, fill beats 2–3 with diatonic/chromatic/arpeggio notes, then overlay shell voicings. Demonstrated over Alone Together and Stompin' At The Savoy.

engine_rules.name: Anchor Walking Bass Root on Beat 1
engine_rules.preference: Always place the chord root on beat 1 of each bar as the foundation of a walking bass line.
engine_rules.falsifier: If the arrangement uses a displaced bass entry (anacrusis/pickup), root may not fall on beat 1.
engine_rules.anchor: Place the root on beat 1 of each bar

engine_rules.name: Add Diatonic or Chromatic Approach Note on Beat 4
engine_rules.preference: On beat 4, place a diatonic or chromatic note that approaches (from above or below) the root of the next bar.
engine_rules.falsifier: If the tempo is too fast or the melody occupies beat 4, the approach note may be omitted.
engine_rules.anchor: Now add either a diatonic or chromatic note on beat 4, above or below the following root note

engine_rules.name: Fill Beats 2 and 3 with Diatonic, Chromatic, or Arpeggio Notes
engine_rules.preference: Complete the four-beat walking line by filling beats 2 and 3 with diatonic scale notes, chromatic passing tones, or arpeggio tones from the current chord.
engine_rules.falsifier: In a two-beat or cut-time feel, beats 2 and 3 may not receive individual bass notes.
engine_rules.anchor: To complete your walking bassline, you just need to add two more notes in between the root note of beat 1, and the approach note of beat 4. These can be any of the following: Diatonic notes from the scale of the given key. Chromatic notes, or Arpeggios.

engine_rules.name: Add Shell Voicings Over Beat-1 Roots in Walking Bass
engine_rules.preference: Once the four-beat walking line is established, layer shell voicings on the root note of each bar to add harmonic content.
engine_rules.falsifier: If the texture is deliberately sparse or the melody is very active, shell voicings may be dropped.
engine_rules.anchor: Now you can add shell voicings on the root notes on each bar.

engine_rules.name: Mix Shell Voicing Placement Between Downbeat and '& of 1'
engine_rules.preference: Alternate shell voicing attacks between the downbeat (beat 1) and the '& of 1' (the upbeat after beat 1) to create rhythmic variety.
engine_rules.falsifier: If a strict, metronomic feel is required, always placing on the downbeat may be preferred.
engine_rules.anchor: It's good to mix up playing them on the downbeat and on the '& of 1' to create variety

engine_rules.name: Substitute Entire Melody Sections with Walking Bass for Contrast
engine_rules.preference: Following Joe Pass's approach, occasionally swap out an entire section's melody and chords and play only walking bass to provide contrast.
engine_rules.falsifier: If the melody is the primary feature throughout, this wholesale substitution would be inappropriate.
engine_rules.anchor: Joe Pass would often swap out an entire section of the melody and only play walking bass, as a way to provide some contrast from the constant melody & chords.

engine_rules.name: Use Walking Bass to Fill Long-Held Melody Notes
engine_rules.preference: When a melody note is held for multiple beats or bars, deploy walking bass beneath it to maintain rhythmic drive and swing.
engine_rules.falsifier: If a still, meditative texture is desired under a long note, walking bass would be inappropriate.
engine_rules.anchor: Notice how the walking bass is used to fill out sections where there is a long-held melody note — this helps keep the drive and swing moving.

engine_rules.name: Apply Walking Bass to Turnaround for Maximum Energy
engine_rules.preference: Walking bass is particularly effective over the I–vi–ii–V turnaround at the end of the A section, where the rapid chord changes create natural walking targets.
engine_rules.falsifier: If the turnaround is played rubato or very slowly, walking bass may not suit the feel.
engine_rules.anchor: It's particularly effective towards the end of the A Section with that I vi ii V turnaround progression

paragraphs.summary: Introduces walking bass as an often-overlooked device for creating energy in solo guitar; notes Joe Pass's practice of substituting entire sections with walking bass.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: Walking bass is an often overlooked way to create more energy and variety in solo guitar arrangements.

sections.title: Passing Chords
sections.summary: Two options for harmonizing additional melody notes beyond primary chord points: (1) diatonic chord dictionary voicings for scale-tone melody notes; (2) chromatic approach chords — play the target voicing then the same voicing one fret away — for accidental/approach melody notes.

engine_rules.name: Harmonize Diatonic Melody Notes with Chord Dictionary Voicings
engine_rules.preference: For diatonic melody notes that need harmonization beyond the primary chord points, use voicings from the chord dictionary; moving voicings through a melody line creates a special effect.
engine_rules.falsifier: If the melody note is non-diatonic (accidental), the chord dictionary alone cannot provide harmonization.
engine_rules.anchor: If you see extra notes you want to harmonize in the melody, and the notes are diatonic, you already have what you need from this course. Simply use voicings from the chord dictionary provided in Appendix 1 to harmonize the melody at additional points.

engine_rules.name: Exploit Moving Voicings Through Melody as Special Effect
engine_rules.preference: Harmonizing multiple consecutive melody notes with individual voicings creates a cool special effect, even if technically complex.
engine_rules.falsifier: If tempo is too fast to execute individual voicings per note, this technique becomes impractical.
engine_rules.anchor: Although this can make things tricky, the voicings moving through a melody line creates a very cool special effect

engine_rules.name: Use Chromatic Approach Chord for Non-Diatonic Approach Notes
engine_rules.preference: When an approach (chromatic/accidental) note appears in the melody, play the target chord voicing then the identical voicing shifted one fret in the direction of the approach note.
engine_rules.falsifier: If the approach note is diatonic, the chromatic one-fret shift may clash with the underlying harmony.

engine_rules.name: Prefer Chromatic Approach Chords When Melody Has Approach Notes
engine_rules.preference: Chromatic approach chords are the best choice specifically when the melody contains an approach note (e.g., bars 4 and 6 of There Is No Greater Love).
engine_rules.falsifier: If the melody moves in purely diatonic steps with no chromatic approach tones, this technique is unnecessary.
engine_rules.anchor: This is a good choice if you have an approach note in the melody, as is the case in There Is No Greater Love on the 4th and 6th bars

engine_rules.preference: For a complete phrase with both diatonic and non-diatonic melody notes, combine option 1 (chord dictionary) and option 2 (chromatic approach) as appropriate note-by-note.
engine_rules.falsifier: If the phrase is entirely diatonic or entirely chromatic, only one technique is needed.

sections.title: Substitution Approach #1 — Tritone Substitution
sections.summary: Tritone substitution — replacing any chord with one whose root is a tritone (3 whole steps, 6 frets) away — is the single most useful harmonic substitution in jazz. C7 and F#7 share guide tones (3rd and 7th swap roles). Demonstrated over Stompin' At The Savoy and Fly Me To The Moon with variants including non-dominant maj7 substitutions and beat-1 plus later-beat deployment.

engine_rules.name: Substitute Any Dominant Chord with Dominant a Tritone Away
engine_rules.preference: Replace any dominant 7 chord with the dominant 7 chord whose root is a tritone (6 semitones) away; this is the single most impactful substitution in jazz arranging.
engine_rules.falsifier: If the root-movement logic of the original progression is critical (e.g., pedagogical context), substitution would obscure it.
engine_rules.anchor: Tritone substitution is the process of substituting one chord for another a tritone away.

engine_rules.name: Exploit Guide-Tone Swap as Justification for Tritone Sub
engine_rules.preference: Recognize that tritone-related dominants share the same 3rd and 7th (guide tones), merely swapping roles — this is the acoustic reason the substitution works.
engine_rules.anchor: C7 has E as the 3rd and Bb as the 7th. F#7 has E as the 7th and A# (which is the same as Bb) as the 3rd. The guide tones have essentially swapped places between these two chords.

engine_rules.name: Apply Tritone-Distance Substitution to Non-Dominant Chords as Experiment
engine_rules.preference: Although tritone substitution strictly applies to dominants, experiment with major and minor chords a tritone away — they can create great effects even if not technically tritone substitution.
engine_rules.falsifier: If the non-dominant tritone sub creates unacceptable dissonance against the melody, revert to original.
engine_rules.anchor: Although this isn't a tritone substitution in the strictest sense (the term usually applied to dominant chords), you can often create great effects by experimenting with major and minor chords as well.

engine_rules.name: Change Dominant Tritone Sub to Maj7 Quality for Softer Color
engine_rules.preference: After placing a dominant tritone sub, experiment with raising the sub to maj7 quality for a softer, more colorful sound.
engine_rules.falsifier: If a strong dominant pull is needed (e.g., approaching a cadence), maj7 quality weakens the resolution.
engine_rules.anchor: Let's see what happens if we make that chord an Emaj7 instead

engine_rules.name: Replace All Substitute Chords with Maj7 Quality for Lush Reharmonization
engine_rules.preference: As an advanced experiment, change all tritone substitutes to maj7 chords to create a lush, harmonically rich reharmonization of the entire passage.
engine_rules.falsifier: If the song is interpreted with a traditional harmonic language, all-maj7 subs would sound too modernist.
engine_rules.anchor: Let's try making ALL the substitute chords maj7 now

engine_rules.name: Deploy Tritone Sub Later in the Bar Rather Than Replacing Beat 1
engine_rules.preference: Play the original chord on beat 1 and introduce the tritone substitution on a later beat within the same bar; this often sounds more natural to the ear than replacing beat 1 outright.
engine_rules.falsifier: If the tritone sub chord carries the melody on beat 1, it must fall on beat 1.
engine_rules.anchor: Another option is to play the original chord on beat 1, then add the tritone substitution later in the bar on other melody notes (this often makes more sense to the ears)

engine_rules.name: Use Tritone Subs Liberally in Solo Guitar (No Ensemble Constraints)
engine_rules.preference: In solo guitar contexts, tritone and other substitutions can be used liberally because there are no other musicians to clash with over the chord changes.
engine_rules.falsifier: When playing with a rhythm section or other musicians who expect standard changes, liberal substitution causes ensemble clashes.
engine_rules.anchor: When it comes to solo guitar, you have the freedom to do these kinds of substitutions liberally as it's just you on stage.

engine_rules.name: Use Substitutions Sparingly — Occasional Brightness, Not Constant Spice
engine_rules.preference: Keep arrangements simple most of the time, adding substitutions occasionally to brighten things; overuse is the equivalent of adding too much spice to a curry.
engine_rules.anchor: Keeping things simple most of the time and just adding a substitution occasionally to brighten up the arrangement is the approach I find works best — a good arrangement is all about subtlety!

engine_rules.name: Find Tritone Root by Moving 6 Frets (3 Whole Steps) Up from Original Root
engine_rules.preference: To locate the tritone substitute root on the guitar, move up (or down) 6 frets from the original chord root — both directions arrive at the same pitch class.
engine_rules.anchor: To find a tritone, start with a note then move upwards 3 tones (which equals 3 whole steps or 6 frets).

sections.title: Substitution Approach #2 — Major Chords to Minor Chords
sections.summary: Two major-to-minor substitutions: (1) Relative substitution — replace chord I with chord vi (e.g., Gmaj7 → Em7), justified by shared key signatures and common tones; (2) Chord I to chord iii substitution (e.g., Gmaj7 → Bm7), where iii is an inversion of Imaj9. Both techniques avoid static bass-root repetition and enable chord addition.

engine_rules.name: Substitute Chord I with Chord vi (Relative Substitution)
engine_rules.preference: Replace the tonic major chord (I) with the vi minor chord of the same key; they share all key signature notes and function interchangeably.
engine_rules.falsifier: If the bass player is outlining the I chord root, replacing with vi creates a harmonic clash.
engine_rules.anchor: Rule: you can replace the I chord of a key with the vi chord of the key.

engine_rules.name: Use Shared Key Signature as Basis for Relative Substitution
engine_rules.preference: Because relative major and minor keys share identical pitch content, their chords can substitute freely for one another.
engine_rules.anchor: If these two keys have the same notes, you can often substitute the chords from those keys for each other. We call this a relative substitution.

engine_rules.name: Substitute Chord I with Chord iii to Avoid Static Root Bass
engine_rules.preference: When the tonic chord is static across multiple bars, substitute chord iii (e.g., Bm7 for Gmaj7) to get away from constant root-tone bass and provide bass-line movement.
engine_rules.falsifier: If the tonic root is the melodic foundation of the section, moving away from it harmonically may destabilize the melody.
engine_rules.anchor: These kinds of substitutions are great to use as it gets you away from being stuck with the root tone in the bass the whole time, which can get a bit stale after a while.

engine_rules.name: Apply Rule: Major Chord → Chord iii of Its Key
engine_rules.preference: Any major chord can be substituted by the minor 7 chord built on the 3rd degree of that major chord's key (e.g., Gmaj7 → Bm7).
engine_rules.falsifier: If the melody note is the root of the original major chord, the iii chord substitution changes the bass note but must still support the melody.
engine_rules.anchor: Rule: you can substitute a major chord for chord iii of its key.

engine_rules.name: Add Extra Chords via Major-to-Minor Substitution (Chord Addition)
engine_rules.preference: Rather than replacing the original chord entirely, add a vi or iii substitute chord in the second bar of a prolonged harmonic area, creating chord addition rather than pure substitution.
engine_rules.falsifier: If the harmonic rhythm is already fast, adding extra chords will crowd the progression.
engine_rules.anchor: This process is referred to as chord addition — adding extra chords to the harmony.

engine_rules.name: Use Major-to-Minor Substitutions to Keep Solo Guitar Fresh and Moving
engine_rules.preference: Keeping things fresh and moving through major-to-minor substitutions is part of the solo jazz guitarist's core role.
engine_rules.anchor: Keeping things fresh and moving is your job as a solo jazz guitarist.

sections.title: Substitution Approach #3 — Minor 7th for Dominant 7th
sections.summary: Derived from Pat Martino's minor conversion concept: any dominant chord can be replaced by the minor 7 chord built on its 5th (equivalent to the iim7 of the dominant). Because ii and V share nearly identical notes (differing by one note), they can be freely interchanged. Demonstrated over a blues in Bb, oscillating between ii and V on key bars.

engine_rules.name: Substitute Dominant 7 with Minor 7 Built on Its 5th
engine_rules.preference: Replace a dominant 7 chord with the minor 7 chord built on the 5th of that dominant (its iim7); they share nearly identical notes and function interchangeably.
engine_rules.falsifier: If the tritone resolution voice-leading of the dominant 7 is critical to the passage, replacing it with iim7 removes that tension.
engine_rules.anchor: You can use a minor 7 chord from the 5th of any dominant chord (which is like using the iim7 that belongs to the dominant chord).

engine_rules.name: Treat ii and V as Interchangeable (Joe Pass Principle)
engine_rules.preference: Because ii and V differ by only one note, follow Joe Pass's practice of interchanging them freely to create variety over either chord.
engine_rules.anchor: Joe Pass would often mention that the ii and the V chord can be interchanged with one another, and this is the reason - they are very similar in their construction.

engine_rules.name: Oscillate ii–V Over Long Dominant Chords to Avoid Stagnation
engine_rules.preference: Over a long dominant chord, move between the ii and V chord to prevent stagnation and create more energy.
engine_rules.falsifier: If the dominant is very brief (one beat), oscillation is not practical.
engine_rules.anchor: By moving chords between ii and V instead of sticking just to the V chord, you can help the music sound less stagnant.

engine_rules.name: Treat Any Dominant as a Temporary V to Find Its ii Substitute
engine_rules.preference: Even if a dominant chord is not the V7 of the overall key, temporarily treat it as a local V and find its ii chord for substitution.
engine_rules.anchor: Even if it's not the V7 chord of the overall key of the tune, I can pretend for a moment that it is chord V, then think of what the ii chord would be in its key.

engine_rules.name: Add Joe Pass Style Triplet Rhythm to ii–V Substitution
engine_rules.preference: Apply a Joe Pass-style triplet rhythmic figure when oscillating between ii and V chords for an authentic bebop jazz feel.
engine_rules.falsifier: If the arrangement is a ballad or rubato, a triplet figure may disrupt the feel.
engine_rules.anchor: Let's add this 'ii V' effect on bar 8 as well, this time with a cool Joe Pass style triplet rhythm.

engine_rules.name: Apply Minor Conversion Concept: Any Chord Can Be Substituted by a Minor Chord
engine_rules.preference: Following Pat Martino's minor conversion concept, any chord in any progression can theoretically be substituted with a minor chord — keep this as a broad creative option.
engine_rules.falsifier: Not all minor substitutions will produce musically effective results; ear-test each case.
engine_rules.anchor: Pat Martino was a great proponent of what's known as the 'minor conversion concept' - a theory that any chord you see in a progression could be substituted for a minor chord instead.

sections.title: Substitution Approach #4 — Back Cycling
sections.summary: Back cycling exploits the circle of 5ths in reverse (cycle of 4ths) to prepend additional dominant or ii–V chords before a target chord, extending and enriching the harmonic approach. Root movement by 4th is the most common in Western music; a ii–V–I is itself a 3-chord back-cycle. Demonstrated on Number 8.

engine_rules.name: Back Cycle: Add Chords Moving Anti-Clockwise Through Circle of 5ths
engine_rules.preference: Extend the approach to any target chord by prepending one or more chords whose roots move anti-clockwise through the circle of 5ths (i.e., each root a 4th above the last), back-cycling into the target.
engine_rules.falsifier: If the harmonic rhythm is already very dense, adding back-cycle chords will crowd the progression.
engine_rules.anchor: The term 'back cycling' refers to the circle of 5ths … When one cycles anti-clockwise (backward) through the cycle of 5ths, we get a sequence of root tones that are separated by the interval of a 4th.

engine_rules.name: Recognize Cycle of 4th Root Movement as Most Common in Western Music
engine_rules.preference: When constructing or analyzing bass lines and chord progressions, recognize that root movement by a 4th (up) or 5th (down) is the most natural and common harmonic motion — back cycling harnesses this.
engine_rules.anchor: This cycle of root notes a 4th apart is the most common root movement in Western music.

engine_rules.name: Recognize ii–V–I as an Instance of Back Cycling
engine_rules.preference: Understand ii–V–I as a three-chord back-cycle (Dm7 → G7 → Cmaj7 moves by 4ths); this insight allows extension of any target chord approach by further back-cycling.
engine_rules.anchor: In fact, a ii V I progression is an example of this 'cycle 4 root movement'

engine_rules.name: Use Back Cycling to Create Interest in a Chord Progression
engine_rules.preference: Back cycling is a common substitution device for solo jazz guitarists to create more interest in a chord progression by extending dominant motion toward a resolution.
engine_rules.falsifier: If the original harmonic progression is already fast-moving, back cycling may over-complicate it.
engine_rules.anchor: 'Back cycling' is another common form of substitution that solo jazz guitarists use to create more interest in a chord progression.

engine_rules.name: Identify Back Cycling in Existing Jazz Standards
engine_rules.preference: When analyzing a jazz standard, look for back-cycling sequences (strings of dominants or ii–V pairs moving by 4ths) — these are common structural features to highlight or embellish in an arrangement.
engine_rules.anchor: You will also see this harmonic device used liberally in common jazz standards.

engine_rules.name: Chord-phrase substitutions can be pre-meditated or spontaneous

engine_rules.falsifier: Progression is not minor ii-V-i

engine_rules.name: Use rubato when playing spontaneous lick / chord-phrase substitutions

engine_rules.name: Arrangement is only 50% of the work; performance preparation is the other 50%
engine_rules.anchor: Arranging a chord melody is only 50% of the work - the other 50% is turning your arrangement into a great performance on your guitar.

engine_rules.name: Metronome practice stage 1: click on every beat
engine_rules.anchor: Have the metronome click on every beat.

engine_rules.name: Metronome practice stage 2: click on beats 1 and 3
engine_rules.anchor: Then try the metronome clicking on beats 1 and 3 only.

engine_rules.falsifier: Non-jazz styles

then.picking.technique: all assigned fingers sound notes simultaneously

engine_rules.falsifier: Using c (pinky) as a primary plucking finger in 2- or 3-string contexts falsifies this assignment (c is explicitly excluded).
engine_rules.anchor: The main ways to pluck adjacent strings is with the p and i fingers, or i and m fingers. For 3 notes at once, it's preferable to use pi m, or i ma

engine_rules.name: 6ths interval string-skip: use pm or ia finger pairs

then.picking.technique: pinch across skipped string; both notes simultaneous

engine_rules.falsifier: Using p+i or i+m for a skipped-string 6th interval (where the intermediate string must be silenced) falsifies the prescribed skip-pair assignment.
engine_rules.anchor: Now you need to negotiate a string skip in the plucking hand, hence the use of pm and ia as marked.

engine_rules.name: Thumb may double-pluck naturally in complex multi-string patterns

picking.finger_assignment.p: may strike same string twice consecutively when pattern logic requires it

then.picking.technique: thumb double-pluck is idiomatic and simplifies picking fingering in Metheny-style 3rds patterns

engine_rules.falsifier: Forcing i or m to take the second consecutive bass note specifically to avoid a thumb double-pluck falsifies the naturalness claim for this pattern type.
engine_rules.anchor: Notice that the thumb plays a note twice in a row. It's quite natural for the thumb to do a double pluck in these situations as it simplifies the picking fingering greatly.

engine_rules.name: All plucked strings must sound simultaneously in block voicings

then.picking.technique: pinch — all assigned fingers release simultaneously so no arpeggiation arises unintentionally

engine_rules.falsifier: Sequential plucking (one finger after another) in a block-chord context falsifies simultaneity requirement.
engine_rules.anchor: ensure that both fingers sound the notes simultaneously

paragraphs.summary: Technique overview for plucking multiple strings: wrist roll, finger pairs for 2- and 3-string, exclusion of c, practice both combinations on repeats.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: Ensure that your wrist is rolled slightly more towards the headstock to allow more space between the index finger and thumb.

sections.title: Three-String Exercises
sections.summary: Four exercises for plucking three strings: block simultaneous plucking, cross-string arpeggio picking, irregular/asymmetric patterns, and thumb-independence in a Giuliani-derived pattern with thumb alternating between strings 5 and 4. Essential for chord melody and comping.

engine_rules.name: Three-string block plucking: all notes exactly simultaneous

then.picking.technique: pinch with p+i+m or i+m+a; all three notes released at exactly the same time

engine_rules.falsifier: Any staggered attack across the three strings in a block-chord context falsifies the simultaneity requirement.
engine_rules.anchor: make sure all notes sound at exactly the same time on each chord

engine_rules.name: Cross-string arpeggio picking: sequential finger release across 3 strings

then.picking.technique: arpeggio — sequential plucking across strings in a repeating cross-string pattern; particularly effective in solo guitar arrangements

engine_rules.falsifier: Playing all three strings simultaneously (block) instead of in sequence falsifies the cross-string arpeggio texture.
engine_rules.anchor: This exercise is excellent for developing cross-string arpeggio picking technique. It's a neat texture that can sound particularly good in solo guitar arrangements.

engine_rules.name: Giuliani pattern: thumb alternates between strings 5 and 4

picking.finger_assignment.p: alternates between string 5 and string 4 throughout pattern

then.picking.technique: thumb independence — p moves between two bass strings while upper fingers maintain consistent treble pattern

engine_rules.falsifier: Keeping the thumb on a single string for the entire Giuliani exercise falsifies the alternation principle.
engine_rules.anchor: It's a great way to develop thumb independence in a picking pattern context — the thumb moves between the 5th and 4th strings as you play the exercise.

engine_rules.name: Irregular/asymmetric patterns increase comping flexibility

then.picking.technique: non-predictable picking sequence (e.g. Barry's Burger) trains adaptability for comping and chord melody beyond regular block or arpeggio patterns

engine_rules.falsifier: Exclusively practising regular (block or ascending arpeggio) patterns while neglecting irregular patterns falsifies the flexibility claim.
engine_rules.anchor: This is a good exercise to play because it's a less predictable picking pattern in the plucking hand. This will give you more flexibility in applying these techniques to your comping and chord melodies.

sections.title: Four-String Exercises
sections.summary: Three exercises for plucking four strings simultaneously or in rapid sequence using all four main fingers (p+i+m+a). Danny Dreamer 1 uses block four-string chords; Danny Dreamer 2 uses sequential plucking of the same voicings; Southern Land uses a 16th-note arpeggio pattern at double speed (more advanced). Pinky (c) explicitly excluded; four-finger maximum.

engine_rules.name: Four-string plucking: p+i+m+a, pinky excluded

then.picking.technique: four strongest fingers only; c reserved for exceptional cases

engine_rules.falsifier: Routinely assigning c to the fourth string instead of a in four-string contexts falsifies the p+i+m+a assignment.
engine_rules.anchor: I rarely use the little finger (c) on the right hand with fingerstyle technique — I tend to stick to 4-note voicings as a maximum which means you will only need to use your four strongest fingers - pi ma.

engine_rules.name: Four-string block chord: all four notes sound simultaneously

then.picking.technique: pinch — all four fingers release simultaneously; no stagger

engine_rules.falsifier: Staggered release of any of the four fingers producing audible arpeggio in Danny Dreamer 1 falsifies simultaneous attack.
engine_rules.anchor: ensure that you're sounding all the notes in each chord at the same time

engine_rules.name: Four-string sequential plucking as variation on block chords

then.picking.technique: arpeggio — same voicings as Danny Dreamer 1 but plucked sequentially (one finger after another) rather than simultaneously

engine_rules.falsifier: Playing Danny Dreamer 2 as a simultaneous block (same as #1) falsifies the sequential/arpeggio contrast intent.
engine_rules.anchor: Here's a variation of the above "Danny the Dreamer" exercise, using sequential plucking instead of block chords.

engine_rules.name: Southern Land: 16th-note four-string arpeggio at double speed — advanced

then.picking.technique: arpeggio — same pattern as Danny Dreamer 2 but in 16th notes (twice as fast); classified as more advanced workout

engine_rules.falsifier: Playing Southern Land at 8th-note speed (same as Danny Dreamer 2) without progressing to 16th notes falsifies the advanced tempo goal.
engine_rules.anchor: the pattern is now twice as fast, incorporating 16th notes, so this is a more advanced workout

paragraphs.summary: Introduction to four-string exercises; same technique feel as three-string but adding a fourth finger; task (5 min/day, master in order). Danny Dreamer 1: block simultaneous four-string chord plucking.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: La pièce de résistance! Now that you've worked out three-string picking, let's try four strings.

paragraphs.summary: Danny Dreamer 2: sequential (arpeggio) variant of Danny Dreamer 1 using the same voicings.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: Here's a variation of the above "Danny the Dreamer" exercise, using sequential plucking instead of block chords.

paragraphs.summary: Southern Land: arpeggio study at 16th-note speed — twice the tempo of Danny Dreamer 2 making it a more advanced exercise.
paragraphs.verbatim_anchor: the pattern is now twice as fast, incorporating 16th notes, so this is a more advanced workout

sections.title: Fingerstyle Etudes
sections.summary: Two extended etudes consolidating all fingerstyle techniques: (1) Walking Bass Bb Blues — walking bassline with chordal accompaniment across a full 24-bar Bb blues; (2) Bossa Nova Comping Etude — ii–V–I sequence moving down by whole steps with bossa nova thumb-plus-fingers picking pattern. Each etude should first be learned chord by chord or bar by bar before combining with full picking pattern.

engine_rules.name: Etude 1: walking bass on lower strings with p; chord accompaniment with i+m+a

then.picking.technique: simultaneous or near-simultaneous p + upper fingers; bass line moves chromatically while upper chord voices sustain or move independently

engine_rules.falsifier: Using i or m exclusively for bass-line notes in this etude while p plays upper voices falsifies the thumb-bass assignment.
engine_rules.anchor: This first etude is a walking bass study over a Bb blues. Although this sort of study is quite well known, it's brilliant for gaining control over plucking multiple strings.

engine_rules.name: Etude 1 learning strategy: one bar at a time

then.picking.technique: isolate and master one bar before joining; do not attempt full run-through until each bar is secure

engine_rules.falsifier: Attempting the full 24-bar etude immediately without bar-by-bar isolation falsifies the prescribed learning order.
engine_rules.anchor: Practice this study one bar at a time, until you can play it all the way through.

engine_rules.name: Etude 2: bossa nova — thumb on bass, fingers on upper strings in syncopated pattern

picking.finger_assignment.p: bass string notes in bossa nova rhythmic pattern
picking.finger_assignment.i_m: upper string chord tones and syncopated melody

then.picking.technique: bossa nova pattern — thumb plays bass independently from upper finger syncopation; thumb independence is primary training goal

engine_rules.falsifier: Playing the bossa nova etude with thumb and fingers locked in unison rhythmically (no independence) falsifies the thumb-independence training purpose.
engine_rules.anchor: This exercise is a great workout for fingerstyle technique and enables you to quickly gain facility in the plucking hand as well as the independence of the thumb.

engine_rules.name: Etude 2 learning strategy: single-chord pattern first, then full ii–V–I

then.picking.technique: step 1: practise picking pattern on one static chord until internalised; step 2: add fretting-hand chord changes across full descending ii–V–I progression

engine_rules.falsifier: Attempting picking pattern and chord changes simultaneously from the first repetition falsifies the two-phase learning sequence.
engine_rules.anchor: I would suggest practicing the picking pattern over a single chord for a while until you get it under your fingers first. After that, start to build the pattern over the full chord progression.

engine_rules.name: Etude 2 harmonic structure: ii–V–I moving down by two frets (whole step) repeatedly

then.voicing.harmonic_motion: ii–V–I cell, transposed down one whole step (two frets) per repetition

engine_rules.falsifier: Transposing by a non-whole-step interval or ascending rather than descending falsifies the stated harmonic direction.
engine_rules.anchor: The exercise comprises a straightforward ii V I sequence, moving down two frets at a time.
